brief.text: Upper-class chil­dren in India tire of each new toy in three days, Ajay Shah said. In his child­hood, twenty chil­dren shared one ten­nis ball. {090-S04}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how limits breed invention
lead.head: Stupid, therefore creative

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 90

body: Ajay Shah opened the episode of­fended. Amit Varma had called him stupid, he com­plained, and in any de­cent age that would have meant a duel at fifty paces.
Varma’s de­fence was that he had called them both stupid. “We are both cre­ative be­cause we are both stupid,” he said. {090-C01}

The brain, he ex­plained, can­not take in all the com­plex­ity of the world. So we tell sto­ries that are sim­pler than re­al­ity, never en­tirely true but use­ful, and our cre­ativ­ity grows out of that limit.

Shah took the point into his own field. A storyteller’s sto­ries and a scientist’s mod­els are the same thing, he said, quot­ing the statis­ti­cian George Box: “All mod­els are wrong, some mod­els are use­ful.”
The theme, Varma an­nounced, was how con­straints can often lead to ex­plo­sions of cre­ativ­ity. What fol­lowed was a run of sto­ries about peo­ple who met a hard limit and found an­other way.
## Limits that made some­thing

Joni Mitchell got polio at nine and her left hand grew much weaker, so she in­vented about fifty al­ter­na­tive gui­tar tun­ings. Frida Kahlo, bedrid­den after a bus ac­ci­dent, painted self-portraits from her bed with the help of a mir­ror her par­ents set up.
Dr Seuss wrote *Green Eggs and Ham* on his publisher’s chal­lenge to use only fifty words. Dick Fosbury could not mas­ter the high jump’s strad­dle, so he in­vented the flop and won Olympic gold.
Coco Chanel could not af­ford silk, so she made cou­ture from jer­sey. Keith Haring drew in chalk in the New York sub­way be­cause he had to fin­ish be­fore the tran­sit po­lice ar­rived.
Varma was care­ful about what he claimed. Polio was no bless­ing to Mitchell, he said, “be­cause no one should get polio”.
But it was a bless­ing to music: “It pushed a per­son, forced a per­son into going into dif­fer­ent di­rec­tions and doing in­ter­est­ing things.” {090-C02}
Shah found the sto­ries in­spir­ing. “In India we have peo­ple who will give you twenty rea­sons why X can’t be done,” he said.
## Forced or cho­sen

Shah drew a line be­tween con­straints the world forces on you, such as polio, and con­straints you choose. Why would any­one play chess blind­fold? Because, he said, “it’s like the con­straint is what brings it to life.” {090-C03}
Varma widened the idea. A gui­tar is a con­straint, he said, and so is a key­board; Shah added the 800-word col­umn and the 280-character tweet. The ques­tion, Varma said, is how you look at it.
## Enter the grinch

Near the end, Shah vol­un­teered to be “the main grinch”. Millions of peo­ple were struck down by polio, he said, and for most it made life worse. We pick the sto­ries of the few who broke out. {090-C10}

His sec­ond cau­tion was math­e­mat­i­cal. Add con­straints to an op­ti­mi­sa­tion prob­lem, and at best you match the un­con­strained an­swer. “If you re­spect the frame, then it’s in­evitable that as you layer on the con­straints, it gets worse,” he said. {090-C09}
Varma was not for a mo­ment say­ing that polio, or con­straints, are good, he replied. The point was to be in­spired by such sto­ries, and to get past our own.

Earlier, he had noted that the show it­self runs within a limit of sixty to ninety min­utes. He signed off ac­cord­ingly: “We will re­spect the con­straints of your time and we will let you go and do amaz­ing things.”

second.label: Children’s books
second.head: Green eggs on a budget
second.deck: Amit Varma on a publisher’s challenge and the children’s book it produced
body: Bennett Cerf, a founder of Random House and Dr Seuss’s pub­lisher, chal­lenged him to write a full book using only fifty words. It could be as long as he liked, Amit Varma ex­plained, but with no more than fifty dif­fer­ent words. {090-S06}

Seuss, whose real name was Theodor Geisel, kept a chart of his words, Varma thinks, and pulled it off with *Green Eggs and Ham*. Varma read it aloud: “I do not like green eggs and ham, I do not like them, Sam I am.” {090-R02}
Asked if he liked green eggs and ham, Ajay Shah said he would be will­ing to try. Varma, who teaches writ­ing, uses the story with stu­dents who fear their vo­cab­u­lary is too small.

quote.text: The idea was you have to write a full book using only fifty words.

third.head: No off side, no problem

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Tendulkar’s missing off side

body: Sachin Tendulkar’s cover drive, Amit Varma said, was per­fec­tion, “ge­om­e­try come to life”. Then Tendulkar got ten­nis elbow, and never re­vealed in pub­lic how bad it was.
Varma has heard, through a very close friend of his who is a very close friend of Tendulkar’s, that at one point he could not lift a cup of tea. A Test against Australia in Sydney lay ahead.
Unable to drive through the off side, Tendulkar de­cided he would do with­out it. “And he makes a dou­ble hun­dred with­out driv­ing through the off­side even once,” Varma said. {090-S10}

It was not an in­no­va­tion story like the oth­ers, Varma con­ceded. He also teased Ajay Shah: a good Indian, “for the pur­pose of this chap­ter”, is some­one who fol­lows cricket, and Shah does not. {090-J07}

sections.label: First story
sections.head: Fifty ways to tune a guitar
sections.caption: Joni Mitchell’s fifty tunings
body: Joni Mitchell got polio at nine, Amit Varma said, and for a long time her left hand was much weaker. She later said it gave her an inner life and turned her into an artist. {090-S01}
For some­one who wanted to make music, that was a se­ri­ous prob­lem. She was a fine pi­anist and could have given up the gui­tar. Instead she came up with about fifty al­ter­na­tive tun­ings.

Her method was to hear a chord in her head that she could not play in the usual tun­ing, and to keep re­tun­ing the strings until the gui­tar pro­duced it. David Crosby, an early men­tor, said her ex­per­i­ments blew his mind.
## An or­ches­tra in six strings

She called the un­usual chords she found “chords of in­quiry”, and heard an en­tire or­ches­tra in six strings, Varma said, with the top three strings like a horn sec­tion. She got to know the in­stru­ment more in­ti­mately than a con­ven­tion­ally trained player.

The re­sult is a sound hard to file: not quite folk, def­i­nitely not quite blues, with plenty of jazz. Had she not got polio, Varma said, she might have learned the gui­tar nor­mally and ex­per­i­mented far less. {090-C02}
~ Mitchell called her­self “a painter de­railed by cir­cum­stance”, though she painted all her own album cov­ers. *Both Sides Now*, Varma noted, is one of Ajay Shah’s favourite songs. {090-J14}

quote.text: It made me have an inner life and it turned me into an artist.
quote.who: Joni Mitchell, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Second story
sections.head: A mirror over the sickbed
sections.caption: Frida Kahlo’s mirror
body: Frida Kahlo got polio at six, Amit Varma said, which left one leg weaker. At eigh­teen, on her way to med­i­cal school, she was in a wooden bus that col­lided with a rail car. A rail­ing went through her pelvis and in­jured her spine. Through her life she faced some thirty-two surg­eries. {#surgeries}
Her dream of be­com­ing a doc­tor was over. Her par­ents en­cour­aged her paint­ing in­stead: they rigged up an easel over her bed, and a mir­ror so she could look at her­self. {090-S03}
The self-portraits fol­lowed. She painted the plas­ter corsets that held her spine to­gether and the equip­ment around her. *The Broken Column*, from 1944, came after a spinal surgery went wrong.
## Time alone
Varma asked whether being forced to spend time with your­self is, in some ways, a bless­ing. He and Ajay Shah grew up with­out the in­ter­net or mo­bile phones.

Sara Rai, Munshi Premchand’s grand­daugh­ter, de­scribed her child­hood to him in vivid de­tail. He won­dered whether los­ing the con­straint of hav­ing noth­ing to do has left us going from sen­sa­tion to sen­sa­tion. {090-C12}
~ Kahlo still lived a full life, Varma said, in­clud­ing a tu­mul­tuous mar­riage to Diego Rivera. He loved an­other line of hers: “Feet, what do I need you for when I have wings to fly.” {090-J13}

quote.text: I paint self por­traits be­cause I am so often alone, be­cause I am the per­son I know best.
quote.who: Frida Kahlo, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: On writing
sections.head: Just the tip of the iceberg
sections.caption: writing within limits
body: Amit Varma’s writ­ing stu­dents often worry that their vo­cab­u­lary is too small. He has two an­swers. Read a lot, and it will grow. And it is al­ready enough, since no writer needs more words than her read­ers know. {090-C05}

Agatha Christie, he said, had dys­graphia and per­haps dys­lexia. Rather than give up, she de­vel­oped a clear, con­cise style and tight, in­tri­cate plot­ting. “Out of that lim­i­ta­tion arises a style that is a fea­ture, not a bug,” Varma said. {090-S07}

Ernest Hemingway’s spare style came partly from fil­ing dis­patches on dead­line. His ice­berg idea held that only about an eighth of what is going on needs to be in the story. “It is not only show don’t tell, but it is show enough and no more,” Varma said. {090-C06}
## Cut to fit
Varma used to com­plain about 800-word col­umn lim­its, write 1,200 words and then find that what he cut was not needed. “You need that ar­ti­fi­cial con­straint to get it done,” he said. {090-C07}
His stu­dents get a final ex­er­cise: no ad­verbs, no ad­jec­tives, no word over two syl­la­bles. The aim, he said, is to make them look at their sen­tences care­fully.
~ The great Hindi film lyri­cists, Sahir Ludhianvi, Gulzar and Javed Akhtar, all wrote to meter and music, he said. The con­straints brought out the ge­nius in their work.

quote.text: I do not be­lieve, Ajay Shah, that any writer needs a greater vo­cab­u­lary than her read­ers.

portraits.caption: Agatha Christie
portraits.credit: Joop van Bilsen for Anefo, CC0

sections.label: In sport
sections.head: A flop that won gold
sections.caption: the Fosbury flop
body: In sport, Amit Varma said, the rules are the con­straints. Limit the field­ers in the out­field in a one-day match, or bring in football’s off­side rule, and you change the in­cen­tives and so the game.

Baseball keeps tin­ker­ing with its rules to keep the game bal­anced, Varma said, the sub­ject of a bril­liant book by Stephen Jay Gould. In a sense it is cen­tral plan­ning, which works be­cause a game is not un­bound­edly com­plex. {090-R08}

At school, Dick Fosbury could not do the strad­dle, in which you face the bar and cross it one leg at a time. So he tried other things and, like all heretics, was mocked. One head­line said “Fosbury flops”, and peo­ple likened him to a fish flop­ping into a boat.
In 1968, he won Olympic gold with the flop, and it be­came the stan­dard tech­nique. {#fosbury}
## Not from first prin­ci­ples
Fosbury did not rea­son his way there from aero­dy­nam­ics, Varma stressed. “He had a con­straint. He sim­ply couldn’t do the strad­dle,” he said. {090-S09}
And the flop spread only once deep foam mat­tresses re­placed sand and shal­low pad­ding, which had made land­ing on your back dan­ger­ous. {090-C08}
~ Varma con­fessed that he had tried the high jump at school, failed and given up. Thinking of Fosbury, he now won­ders what might have hap­pened had he per­se­vered.

quote.text: The Fosbury flop might have been in­cen­tivized by a con­straint. But the suc­cess of it was in­cen­tivized by the re­moval of a con­straint.

sections.label: Mini stories
sections.head: Weak glue, strong idea
sections.caption: the Post-it note
body: Amit Varma ended with a run of mini sto­ries, cred­it­ing Vaishnav Vyas and Nomsita MS Haritashya as co-creators of the episode.

Spencer Silver of 3M set out to make the strong­est ad­he­sive known to man, and failed. One at­tempt was a spec­tac­u­lar fail­ure, a re­ally weak ad­he­sive. Using it gave him the idea for the Post-it note. {090-S13}

Post-its are now so com­mon, Varma said, that soft­ware shows vir­tual ones. That is skeuo­mor­phic de­sign: new tech­nol­ogy bor­rows the look of the old, as when a books app looks like a book­shelf or a save but­ton shows a floppy disk. It eases peo­ple in, but can out­stay its wel­come.
## Constraints by choice

Some con­straints are cho­sen. Apple, Varma said, set it­self tar­gets for how thin and light the MacBook Air would be that ex­ist­ing tech­nol­ogy could not meet, and then built the tools to meet them. {#macbook}
Then he set home­work: think about the con­straints of the artists, sci­en­tists and writ­ers you ad­mire, and about the ones that have stopped you from even at­tempt­ing some­thing.

~ Ajay Shah, mean­while, still owes rec­om­men­da­tions. He had promised five for this episode; when he tried to defer, Varma threat­ened to de­mand ten, and they set­tled on six for the next. {#promise}

quote.text: But that weak ad­he­sive when he uses it, it gives him an idea.

I won­der in mod­ern times if the ab­sence of the con­straint called noth­ing to do has made us into crea­tures who are going from sen­sa­tion to sen­sa­tion and not spend­ing enough time with our­selves.

p3.deck: Four people, four constraints, and what each one made of it

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s IIT story, and a high score built on a fracture
stories.head: Can’t play the game? Rewrite it
body: In Ajay Shah’s stu­dent days at IIT, the most im­por­tant male ob­jec­tive, he said, was a key­board game called Digger. Amit Varma was ap­palled. “What kind of male ob­jec­tive is that? Shame on you,” he said. {090-J08}

Digger stored its high scores, en­crypted, on a floppy disk, and a student’s brag­ging rights de­pended en­tirely on that num­ber. Then Shah suf­fered mul­ti­ple com­pound frac­tures of his right arm. He was right-handed, and games were played on the key­board.

With noth­ing bet­ter to do, he dis­as­sem­bled the game’s com­piled bi­nary and read it, hun­dreds of times. He knew the game in­ti­mately, and slowly he found the re­gions of the file where the floor plan of each level was stored.
He found he could change them, so he wrote an ed­i­tor to de­sign his own lev­els. Then he built one in which the mon­sters died by them­selves, and left the ma­chine run­ning all night.
“The world cham­pi­ons at the time had like scores of ten, twenty thou­sand and I re-emerged from my frac­tured right arm days with a high score of three hun­dred thou­sand,” Shah said. {090-S11}
“At one level this might be called adapt­ing to con­straints,” Varma said. “Fancy term. This is cheat­ing.” Shah said it was the only time in his life he had read bi­nary.

~ Varma asked the ed­i­tor, Nomsita, to leave the whole story in and “let the world see what a shame­less man this is”. Then he re­lented: “At one level I just lost re­spect for you, but at an­other level I gained re­spect for you.”
stories.why: Shut out of the game, Shah went a level up and rewrote its lev­els. Varma called it cheat­ing. Either way, the con­straint sent Shah some­where he would not oth­er­wise have gone: into the game’s bi­nary.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Digger hack

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a Hindi writer who never waited for quiet
stories.head: Serve dinner, then write
body: When Amit Varma’s writ­ing stu­dents say they have no time, he tells them about Shivani, a leg­endary Hindi writer of the mid-twentieth cen­tury. Women es­pe­cially, he said, carry a dou­ble load of ca­reer, cook­ing and chil­dren.

Shivani’s daugh­ter Mrinal Pande told Varma how her mother worked. Shivani would cook, serve the whole fam­ily, and then sit down and write as they ate around her. The fam­ily knew not to dis­turb her.

She did not wait for a va­ca­tion, or wake up four hours early for quiet. Varma put her rea­son­ing in her own voice: “Whatever lit­tle scraps of time I get within that, I will just sit and write.” {090-S02}
~ Varma has in­ter­viewed both of Shivani’s daugh­ters, Mrinal Pande and Ira Pande, and her nephew Pushpesh Pant, who was like a son to her.

quote.text: Everyone is con­strained. So at some point you’re alive, you’re breath­ing, you’re lucky, just stop com­plain­ing and get on with it.

stories.postscript: Varma has taught more than 2,800 stu­dents in his on­line writ­ing course. {#students}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Shivani at the dinner table

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a designer who could not afford silk
stories.head: Couture from the underwear drawer
body: Coco Chanel came from a rel­a­tively hum­ble fam­ily, Amit Varma said. In the early twen­ti­eth cen­tury she wanted to be a fash­ion de­signer, but could not af­ford the silks and bro­cades of high fash­ion.
So her early ex­per­i­ments used cheaper ma­te­rial such as jer­sey, which was then used to make men’s un­der­wear. {#jersey} Out of it she made classy women’s gar­ments.
That was not typ­i­cally done. But it made her clothes cheaper, and so more af­ford­able and ac­ces­si­ble. {090-S14}

~ What later be­came com­mon­place in fash­ion, Varma said, began with one person’s con­straint. In his telling, her think­ing went: “I can’t do high fash­ion with silks and bro­cades, but I can do beau­ti­ful cou­ture with other gar­ments and bring them to the fore.”
stories.why: Lacking ex­pen­sive ma­te­ri­als did not stop Coco Chanel; it pointed her to a new kind of el­e­gance that more peo­ple could af­ford. What began as one designer’s bud­get be­came some­thing com­mon across fash­ion.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Coco Chanel’s jersey

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on art made in a hurry, before the police came
stories.head: Chalk it up to the transit police
body: In the early 1980s, Keith Haring was an art stu­dent in New York, Amit Varma said. Rather than sell elit­ist paint­ings to gal­leries, he wanted to paint out­doors.
The sub­way of­fered him a sur­face. When an ad­ver­tise­ment ex­pired, it was cov­ered with black can­vas. {#canvas} That, Varma said, was the ideal can­vas for Haring.

But he had to hurry, to fin­ish be­fore the tran­sit po­lice came, and he needed a ma­te­rial that suited speed. So he used chalk. {090-S15} His style adapted to the pace, the medium, the pub­lic set­ting and the cer­tainty that the work would soon be gone.

~ Out of it came quick mo­tifs, such as his bark­ing dog, that be­came iconic and were copied by oth­ers. Later, fa­mous, he was com­mis­sioned to paint grand mu­rals that would last. The style stayed.
stories.why: Having to hurry worked like a de­sign brief. The con­di­tions of fast, un­of­fi­cial pub­lic draw­ing gave Haring a vis­ual vo­cab­u­lary that later be­came iconic, and stayed with him even when the hurry was over.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 90. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Frida Kahlo (Guillermo Kahlo, public domain); Joni Mitchell (Library of Congress Life, CC0); Dr. Seuss (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Agatha Christie (Joop van Bilsen for Anefo, CC0); Ernest Hemingway (Lloyd Arnold, public domain); Dick Fosbury (Wikimedia Commons, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.why: Sara Rai’s strik­ingly de­tailed child­hood mem­o­ries, and her ex­pla­na­tion that ‘we had noth­ing else to do, so we looked at things’, which in­spired Amit’s ar­gu­ment that un­filled time sharp­ens at­ten­tion.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Mrinal Pande (Episode 263, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A first-hand por­trait of a leg­endary Hindi writer who wrote within the con­straints of run­ning a house­hold.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of Ira Pande (Episode 369, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Another first-hand view of Shivani and her fam­ily.

shelf.title: Pushpesh Pant Feasts on the Buffet of Life (Episode 326, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A re­mark­able con­ver­sa­tion in which Pushpesh Pant urges Indians to ex­plore their own country’s food di­ver­sity, shar­ing the imag­ined maps in his head (re­gions mapped by their sour­ing agent) and how ‘clas­si­cally Indian’ in­gre­di­ents came from out­side.

shelf.title: Life’s Grandeur: The Spread of Excellence From Plato to Darwin
shelf.creator: Stephen Jay Gould
shelf.why: He calls it bril­liant on how base­ball keeps ad­just­ing its rules to keep the game bal­anced.

shelf.title: The Changing Forms of Creativity (Episode 72, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How form shapes con­tent: the venue shapes the music, from per­cus­sion in the open air to none in echo­ing gothic churches to al­ter­na­tive rock in CBGB’s crowded room.

shelf.title: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Episode 68, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The full story of in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, which Ajay pushed for from the 1990s and which took more than fif­teen years to be­come law: a les­son in how slowly good pol­icy ar­rives.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: Ajay opens of­fended at being called stupid, say­ing that in any de­cent age he would have slapped Amit with a glove and fought a duel at fifty paces ‘with rusty guns that barely aim ac­cu­rately.’ Amit, the lib­er­tar­ian, replies: ‘So much talk about the co­er­cion of the state, mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence. Are you the state that you can threaten me with vi­o­lence?’

Amit ac­cuses Ajay of hi­jack­ing his rec­om­men­da­tion of Derek and the Dominos’ ‘Layla’ the pre­vi­ous week: ‘quite cre­ative, any­thing but stupid, but deeply de­vi­ous.’ He also notes that Vaishnav Vyas calls the Inflation Targeting episode ‘the in­flam­ma­tion tar­get­ing episode.’

Showing view­ers a Dr Seuss page that Ajay can’t see, Amit com­pares it to a chess broad­cast, where ev­ery­one sees the en­gine eval­u­a­tion ex­cept the two play­ers: ‘So they are the two chutiyas who don’t know the right move. Everybody else does.’

On the Digger saga, Amit first asks of the ‘most im­por­tant male objective’ at IIT: ‘What kind of male ob­jec­tive is that? Shame on you.’ When Ajay men­tions break­ing his right hand, Amit adds a fam­ily-show aside that ‘it’s much bet­ter for a male en­gi­neer to in­jure his right hand than his left hand.’ Then: ‘At one level this might be called adapt­ing to con­straints. Fancy term. This is cheat­ing.’ Finally: ‘Nomsita, leave this in... let the world see what a shame­less man this is... at one level I just lost re­spect for you, but at an­other level I gained re­spect for you.’
Amit calls Everything is Everything a work of art made within a 60–90 minute limit: ‘Aren’t you still watch­ing? If you’re still watch­ing, you can’t diss.’
Douglas Adams: ‘I love dead­lines, es­pe­cially the sound they make as they go whoosh­ing by,’ quoted by Amit on dead­lines as a con­straint of time.

Examples of great writ­ing under con­straint: Shakespeare, Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address (‘in one sixty seven words or something’), and Hindi film lyri­cists Sahir Ludhianvi, Gulzar and Javed Akhtar writ­ing to meter and music.
